There is no native speaker in any meeting I chair. My head of claims is Italian, my pricing lead is Colombian, my reinsurance team sits in Poland, and I am Dutch. English belongs to nobody in that room, and the standard is not London or New York. The standard is whether the four of us leave with the same understanding. I have watched people arrive with beautiful, fast, idiomatic English and lose the room in ten minutes, because idiom is exactly what does not survive the crossing. The colleagues who do well slow down by about ten percent, avoid the clever phrase, and say the level of commitment out loud. Not we will look at it, which means four different things in four countries. Something closer to this is a decision, this is an intention, or this is a preference. That habit is worth more than any accent.

For a long time I thought that being clear meant being direct, and I was proud of it. Then I spent two years working with colleagues who never say no, and I discovered that I had been mistaking politeness for agreement, and building plans on it. The sentence that taught me was that would be difficult. I heard hesitation. It was a refusal, delivered exactly as it should have been, and I was the one who could not read it. What changed my results was not becoming indirect. It was learning to ask the second question. When you say difficult, are you telling me it does not work? Written down it looks almost rude, and in practice people are relieved, because you have given them a way to say the thing without losing face. I still choose my own register. I simply stopped assuming that mine is the neutral one.
